q: Which part of the computer is known as its "brain"?
x: The CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions and controls the other parts. The hard disk only stores data, the monitor only displays output and the power supply only provides electricity.

q: Which of the following is an output device?
x: A printer takes information from the computer and produces it on paper. The keyboard, scanner and microphone all send data into the computer, so they are input devices.

q: How many bits make one byte?
x: One byte is a group of 8 bits and can store one character in ASCII. Four bits is a nibble, and 16 bits is two bytes.

q: The base of the binary number system is:
x: Binary uses only the two digits 0 and 1, so its base is 2. Base 8 is octal, base 10 decimal and base 16 hexadecimal.

q: Which unit is used to measure the speed of a processor?
x: Clock speed is measured in hertz, and modern processors are rated in gigahertz. Kilobytes measure storage, megapixels measure image resolution and decibels measure sound.

q: Which of the following is system software?
x: System software manages the hardware and runs other programs; an operating system is the main example. Word processors, spreadsheets and games are application software used for user tasks.

q: Which memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
x: RAM is volatile, so its data disappears without power. ROM, hard disks and flash drives keep their data when the power goes off.

q: What is the hexadecimal digit that stands for the decimal value 10?
x: Hexadecimal counts 0–9 and then A = 10, B = 11 up to F = 15. F is 15, and a digit "1" is simply one.

q: Which component performs arithmetic and logical operations inside the CPU?
x: The ALU carries out additions, subtractions and comparisons such as AND and OR. The control unit only directs the flow of instructions and data, and cache stores copies of data.

q: Which device is used to point at and select items on the screen?
x: A mouse is a pointing input device that moves a cursor and selects items. A speaker, plotter and projector are output devices.

q: The full form of ROM is:
x: ROM stands for Read Only Memory because its contents are normally fixed by the maker and are read but not changed during ordinary use.

q: The binary number 1011 equals which decimal number?
x: Working from the right: 1×1 + 1×2 + 0×4 + 1×8 = 11. The value 13 is 1101, which is a reversed reading of the digits.

q: In which order does the CPU repeat its basic instruction cycle?
x: The CPU first fetches the instruction from memory, then decodes what it means and finally executes it. Executing before decoding is impossible because the operation is unknown until decoded.

q: Which of the following is a programming language?
x: Python is a programming language. Linux is an operating system, Chrome is a browser and Ethernet is a networking technology.

q: Which of these is a storage device?
x: A hard disk stores data permanently. A webcam and joystick are input devices and a monitor is an output device.

q: The decimal number 25 equals which binary number?
x: Divide by 2 repeatedly: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1, so the bits for 16, 8 and 1 are set, giving 11001. The binary 10111 is 23.

q: Which of the following is a function of the control unit?
o: Directing the operation of the processor and other parts
Storing user files permanently on a disk
Displaying text and images on the screen
Converting analogue signals into digital form
x: The control unit coordinates the fetching and execution of instructions and signals other components. It does not store files or drive the display.

q: A set of instructions that tells the computer what to do is called a:
x: A program is a sequence of instructions that a computer executes. A protocol is a set of communication rules, a packet is a unit of network data and a port is a connection point.

q: The smallest unit of data in a computer is a:
x: A bit (binary digit) holds a single 0 or 1 and is the smallest unit. A byte has 8 bits, and words and records are larger groups.

q: The hexadecimal number 2F equals which decimal number?
x: 2F = 2×16 + 15 = 47. The value 62 comes from adding the digits wrongly as 2×16 + 15×2.

q: The physical parts of a computer are called:
x: Hardware means the physical, touchable components such as the CPU and keyboard. Software is the programs that run on them.

q: Which of the following is a secondary storage device?
x: A DVD stores data permanently outside the main memory, so it is secondary storage. Cache, registers and RAM are fast primary storage close to the CPU.

q: The result of binary addition 1101 + 0011 is:
x: 13 + 3 = 16, which is 10000 in binary. Adding column by column with carries: 1+1 = 10 carry 1 and the carry runs through every column. The option 10010 is 18.

q: Which one of the following is NOT an input device?
x: A monitor shows output. A barcode reader, touchpad and light pen send data into the computer.

q: A group of 1,024 bytes is called a:
x: One kilobyte is 1,024 bytes (2¹⁰). A megabyte is 1,024 kilobytes and the larger units follow the same step.

q: Which of the following is the octal equivalent of the binary number 101110?
x: Group the bits in threes from the right: 101 = 5 and 110 = 6, giving 56. Grouping in fours would be hexadecimal, not octal.

q: Which of the following is an example of a high-level language?
x: Java is a high-level language, close to human language and independent of the hardware. Machine and assembly languages are low-level and tied to the processor.

q: Which of these is an example of a non-volatile memory?
x: ROM retains its contents without power. Cache, DRAM and registers are volatile and lose data when power is removed.

q: How many different values can be represented with 3 bits?
x: Each bit has two states, so 3 bits give 2³ = 8 combinations (000 to 111). Six comes from 2×3, which is incorrect.

q: A touchscreen works as:
o: An input device only, since it senses touch
An output device only, since it shows images
Both an input and an output device
A permanent storage device for user files
x: A touchscreen displays information (output) and senses touch (input). That is why it cannot be classed as only one.

q: Which of the following is an optical storage medium?
x: A CD-ROM stores data as pits read by a laser, so it is optical. Tape and floppy disks are magnetic and flash drives use electronic memory chips.

q: Which scheme assigns a unique code to each character so computers can store text?
x: ASCII maps characters to numbers (for example A = 65). HTML marks up web pages, JPEG compresses images and HTTP is a web protocol.

q: Which of the following would be the best use of a plotter?
o: Typing long letters and reports quickly
Scanning old photographs into the computer
Recording sound from a room as a file
x: A plotter draws large, precise line drawings on big paper, as in CAD work. It cannot scan or record.

q: A hard disk that is divided into tracks and sectors stores data by using:
x: A hard disk records bits as magnetised regions on spinning platters, organised in tracks and sectors. Laser pits are used on optical discs and flash cells in SSDs.

q: Decimal 45 converted to hexadecimal is:
x: 45 ÷ 16 = 2 remainder 13, and 13 is D, so the number is 2D. The value 3D equals 61.

q: Which of the following is a pointing device?
x: A touchpad moves a cursor by finger movement, so it is an input pointing device. The others are output devices.

q: Which of the following is the main purpose of a "cache" in a CPU?
o: To store the operating system permanently on the chip
To connect the computer to a wireless network
To convert source code into machine code
To reduce the time taken to access frequently used data
x: Cache keeps copies of recently used instructions and data so the CPU need not wait for slower RAM. It is not permanent storage.

q: The binary number 11001 equals which decimal number?
x: 16 + 8 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 25. The number 27 is 11011, which has an extra 2.

q: Which of the following is an application software?
x: A spreadsheet is used directly for user tasks. The BIOS, device drivers and operating system manage the machine itself.

q: If 1 GB = 1,024 MB and 1 MB = 1,024 KB, how many kilobytes are in 2 GB?
x: 2 GB = 2 × 1,024 MB = 2,048 MB, and 2,048 × 1,024 KB = 2,097,152 KB. The value 1,048,576 is the figure for 1 GB only.

q: The decimal number 18 equals which binary number?
x: 18 = 16 + 2, so the bits for 16 and 2 are set, giving 10010. The value 01001 is 9.

q: Which of the following gives the correct order of memory units from smallest to largest?
x: Each unit is 1,024 times the previous one: byte, KB, MB, GB, TB. The other orders swap adjacent units.

q: A hexadecimal number system has how many different digit symbols?
x: Hexadecimal uses 0–9 and A–F, which makes 16 symbols. Fifteen would leave out the digit 0.

q: A student has a 64 GB flash drive and wants to store 8 MB photos. About how many photos can it hold, taking 1 GB = 1,024 MB?
x: 64 GB = 64 × 1,024 MB = 65,536 MB, and 65,536 ÷ 8 = 8,192 photos. Using 1,000 instead of 1,024 would give 8,000 only, and 6,400 does not match.

q: Which of the following statements about RAM is correct?
o: It is used to store the BIOS permanently
It stores data and programs currently in use
It can be written only once at the factory
It is slower than a hard disk drive for access
x: RAM is the working memory where active programs and data are kept. The BIOS lives in non-volatile memory, and RAM is much faster than a disk.

q: A teacher types students' marks into a computer, the computer calculates each student's average, and a result sheet is printed. Calculating the averages belongs to which stage of the information-processing cycle?
x: Working on the data to produce new results (here, averages) is processing. Typing the marks is input and printing the sheet is output.

q: Answer sheets on which students fill in circles with a pencil are read automatically by which device?
x: An OMR senses the dark marks made in fixed positions on a sheet, which is how MCQ answer sheets are marked. MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on bank cheques.

q: Which kind of language can the CPU carry out directly, without any translator?
x: Machine language is written in binary (0s and 1s) and is the only language the CPU executes directly. Assembly language uses mnemonics and still needs an assembler, and a high-level language needs a compiler or interpreter.

q: Which program converts a program written in assembly language into machine code?
x: An assembler translates assembly-language mnemonics into machine code. Compilers and interpreters translate high-level languages.

q: A disk defragmenter and an antivirus program are both examples of:
o: Utility programs, a kind of system software
Input devices attached to the computer
x: Utility programs maintain and protect the computer, and books class them as system software. They do not translate code and they are not office application packages.

q: Which of the following is an impact printer?
x: A dot-matrix printer forms characters by pins striking an inked ribbon against the paper, so it is an impact printer. Laser, inkjet and thermal printers do not strike the paper.

q: Output shown on a monitor screen, which is lost when the screen is switched off, is called:
x: Output on a screen is soft copy because it is not permanent. Hard copy is output printed on paper.

q: At an ATM, a customer inserts a card, types a PIN, the machine checks the account balance and then gives out cash and a printed receipt. Which statement correctly labels two of these steps?
o: Checking the balance is input; giving out cash is processing
Inserting the card is output; typing the PIN is storage
Printing the receipt is processing; checking the balance is output
Typing the PIN is input; printing the receipt is output
x: The PIN enters the machine, so it is input, and the receipt comes out to the user, so it is output. Checking the balance is processing, not input, which rules out the second statement.

q: A device driver is best described as:
o: Application software that a user runs to draw diagrams
A hardware part that plugs into the motherboard
System software that lets the operating system control a hardware device
A cable that carries signals from the computer to a printer
x: A device driver is a program that tells the operating system how to work a particular device such as a printer. It is software, not a hardware part or a cable.

q: Which list contains only system software?
o: Operating system, word processor, device driver
Web browser, device driver, operating system
x: The operating system, device drivers and language translators such as compilers all manage the computer or help build programs, so they are system software. A word processor, spreadsheet, presentation program and web browser are application software.

q: Which list contains only input devices?
x: A scanner, microphone and joystick all send data into the computer. Each other list has an output device in it: a speaker, a monitor or a printer.

q: A scanner changes a printed photograph into:
o: A hard copy printed on paper
Digital data that the computer can store
Sound that plays through the speakers
x: A scanner is an input device that turns an image on paper into digital data. Producing a printed hard copy is the job of a printer.

q: A school computer stores every student's marks. The principal receives a one-page report listing the top five students worked out from those marks. Which statement is correct?
o: The marks are information and the report is data
Both are data, because both are kept on the computer
Both are information, because both contain numbers
The marks are data and the report is information
x: Data are raw facts (the marks); information is processed, meaningful output (the top-five report). Being stored or containing numbers does not decide which is which.

q: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
x: The program counter keeps the address of the next instruction. The IR holds the current instruction itself, not an address.

q: Which register holds the instruction that the CPU is currently decoding and executing?
x: After fetching, the instruction is placed in the IR for decoding and execution. The PC already points to the next instruction.

q: Which bus carries a memory address from the CPU to the main memory?
x: The address bus carries the location the CPU wants to read or write. The data bus carries the contents and the control bus carries signals such as read and write.

q: Signals such as 'memory read' and 'memory write', which tell memory what to do, travel on the:
x: The control bus carries command and timing signals like read and write. The address bus only carries the location and the data bus only the values.

q: Which statement about the data bus and the address bus is correct?
o: Both buses carry signals in both directions at all times
The data bus is two-way; the address bus is normally one-way, from the CPU
The address bus is two-way; the data bus is one-way, from the CPU
Both buses carry only read and write control signals
x: Data moves both into and out of the CPU, so the data bus is bidirectional, while addresses are sent out by the CPU, so the address bus is unidirectional. Read and write signals belong to the control bus.

q: A CPU has a 16-line address bus. How many different memory locations can it address?
x: Each line is one bit, so 16 lines give 2¹⁶ = 65,536 addresses. The value 256 is 2⁸, for an 8-line bus, and 32,768 is 2¹⁵.

q: How many address lines are needed to address exactly 4,096 memory locations?
x: 2¹² = 4,096, so 12 lines are needed. 10 lines give only 2¹⁰ = 1,024 locations, and 16 lines give 65,536.

q: In a simple accumulator-based CPU, the result of an ALU operation is normally placed in which register?
x: The accumulator holds one operand and receives the ALU's result. The PC and MAR hold addresses and the IR holds the instruction.

q: A simple CPU runs these instructions in order on its accumulator: LOAD 6, ADD 9, SUB 4, ADD 2. LOAD puts the number into the accumulator; ADD and SUB add or subtract the number. What does the accumulator hold at the end?
x: 6, then 6 + 9 = 15, then 15 − 4 = 11, then 11 + 2 = 13. The value 2 comes from treating the last instruction as a LOAD, and 11 stops one step early.

q: During the decode step of the instruction cycle, the control unit:
o: Copies the instruction from memory into the CPU
Carries out the addition in the ALU
Works out which operation the instruction asks for
Writes the result back to the hard disk
x: Decoding interprets the instruction so the control unit knows what to do. Copying it from memory is the fetch step and doing the addition is the execute step.

q: Which sequence correctly describes the fetch step of the instruction cycle?
o: Instruction is copied to IR; PC's address is copied to MAR; the instruction is read into MDR; PC is increased
PC's address is copied to MAR; the instruction is read into MDR; MDR is copied to IR; PC is increased
The instruction is read into MDR; MDR is copied to IR; PC's address is copied to MAR; PC is increased
MDR is copied to MAR; PC's address is copied to IR; the instruction is read into MDR; PC is increased
x: Memory must first be given the address (PC to MAR), then the instruction arrives in the MDR, then it moves to the IR for decoding. Each other order reads or copies the instruction before memory has been given its address.

q: A program checks whether x is greater than y. Which part of the CPU actually compares the two values?
x: Comparisons are logical operations, which the ALU performs. The control unit directs the steps but does not do the comparison itself.

q: CPU registers are:
o: Small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU
Large, slow storage areas on the hard disk
Memory chips on a plug-in expansion card
Parts of ROM that hold the start-up program
x: Registers are tiny high-speed storage places within the processor that hold data and instructions being worked on. They are faster than cache or RAM, not slower like a disk.

q: A processor's clock runs at 2 GHz. How long does one clock cycle take?
x: 2 GHz is 2 × 10⁹ cycles per second, so one cycle lasts 1 ÷ (2 × 10⁹) s = 0.5 × 10⁻⁹ s = 0.5 ns. The value 2 ns would be the cycle time of a 0.5 GHz clock.

q: Compared with an 8-bit data bus running at the same speed, a 16-bit data bus can:
o: Address twice as many memory locations
Transfer twice as many bits at a time
Run the clock at twice the frequency
Store twice as much data on the disk
x: Data bus width sets how many bits move in one transfer, so 16 lines carry twice as many as 8. The number of addressable locations depends on the address bus, not the data bus.

q: Saying that a processor is '64-bit' means that it:
o: Can process 64 bits as one unit at a time
x: The bit size is the word size, the number of bits the CPU handles as one unit. It says nothing about the register count, clock speed or RAM fitted.

q: Which register holds the address of the memory location that is about to be read or written?
x: The MAR holds the address being accessed right now, which may be data as well as an instruction. The PC only holds the address of the next instruction.

q: When a word is read from memory, it first arrives in which register?
x: The MDR (also called the memory buffer register) holds the value that has just come from memory or is about to be written. The MAR holds only the address.

q: Each memory address holds one instruction. An ordinary instruction (not a jump) at address 300 has just been fetched. What does the program counter hold now?
x: After a fetch the PC is increased to point to the next instruction, 300 + 1 = 301. The value 300 is the address of the instruction already fetched.

q: Each memory address holds one instruction. The instruction at address 300 is 'JUMP 450', which moves the program to address 450. After it has executed, what does the program counter hold?
x: A jump loads its target address into the PC, so the next fetch is from 450. The value 301 is what the PC held just after the fetch, before the jump was executed.

q: Which list is in order from fastest to slowest?
x: Registers are inside the CPU and fastest, cache comes next, then main memory (RAM), and a hard disk is slowest. Cache is faster than RAM, which is why it is used to speed up memory access.

q: Which type of ROM can be erased by exposing it to ultraviolet light and then programmed again?
x: EPROM is erased with ultraviolet light. EEPROM is erased electrically, while PROM and mask ROM cannot be erased.

q: Which type of RAM must be refreshed many times every second to keep its data?
x: DRAM stores bits as charges in tiny capacitors that leak, so it must be refreshed. SRAM holds its bits in flip-flops and needs no refreshing.

q: Cache memory is usually made of SRAM rather than DRAM because SRAM:
o: Is cheaper and holds more bits per chip
Keeps its data when the power is off
Can be erased with ultraviolet light
Is faster and needs no refreshing
x: SRAM is faster than DRAM and does not need refreshing, which suits cache. It is more expensive and less dense, and like all RAM it is volatile.

q: Why is magnetic tape slow for finding one record in the middle of the tape?
o: It has random access, so every record must be checked in turn
It is volatile, so the data must be reloaded each time
It is optical, so the laser must refocus for each record
It has sequential access, so the data before it must be passed first
x: Tape is read in sequence from the start, so reaching a middle record means winding past the earlier data. A disk allows direct (random) access to any track.

q: (157)₈ equals which decimal number?
(B6)₁₆ equals which binary number?
x: Each hex digit becomes 4 bits: B = 1011 and 6 = 0110, giving 10110110. Check: B6 = 11 × 16 + 6 = 182 and 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182; 11010110 uses 1101, which is D, not B.

q: (11101011)₂ equals which hexadecimal number?
x: Group in fours from the right: 1110 = E and 1011 = B, giving EB. Check: 128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 2 + 1 = 235 and 14 × 16 + 11 = 235; BE swaps the two groups.

q: The decimal number 100 equals which octal number?
x: 100 ÷ 8 = 12 r 4, 12 ÷ 8 = 1 r 4, 1 ÷ 8 = 0 r 1; reading the remainders from the last gives 144. Check: 64 + 32 + 4 = 100; 441 reads the remainders in the wrong order.

q: (725)₈ equals which hexadecimal number?
x: In binary, 7 = 111, 2 = 010, 5 = 101, giving 111010101; regrouped in fours from the right this is 1 1101 0101 = 1D5. Check: 7 × 64 + 2 × 8 + 5 = 469 and 256 + 13 × 16 + 5 = 469.

q: Which of the following has the largest value?
(3A)₁₆ equals which octal number?
x: 3 = 0011 and A = 1010, giving 00111010; regrouped in threes from the right this is 111 010 = 72₈. Check: 3 × 16 + 10 = 58 and 7 × 8 + 2 = 58, so 58 is the decimal value, not the octal one.
